name: Safrano Pink
lede: Safrano Pink is a pale, warm pink from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of color, closer to peach than to a true pink.

sections.title: A pink that leans toward peach
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color records this hue on plate 1, swatch B9, and the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 cites the same entry and classifies it as a moderate yellowish pink, about two units from the block's center [1]. Its Munsell notation is 0.8YR 8.3/5.0, a very light, low-chroma hue sitting right at the border between the yellow-red and red hue families [1].

The books read give no story for the name itself, and its origin is undocumented here [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[shrimp-pink]], [[melon]] and [[flesh-color]], at 3.6, 4.9 and 5.3 ΔE [1]. The hue also sits near [[salmon]] and [[apricot]], two other pale, warm pinks in our library [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Safrano Pink covers at least one per cent of the canvas in 31 paintings, about 0.13 per cent overall; the within-painting lens, which looks at color role regardless of area, finds it in 14 [2]. That makes it rarer than about 65 per cent of the named colors in the archive [2]. When it does appear, it is most often cast as a light tone, in half of those 14 paintings, a pattern area alone could not fake [2].

The earliest dated painting to carry it is from 1495, by the Master of Apollo and Daphne, with the third-earliest from 1522 and the latest from 1941, 23 dated paintings in all, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. That is 435 years before the name's own earliest record, in 1930, so the match is a look-alike hue caught in an aged photograph, not evidence that Maerz and Paul's pigment or dye was already in use [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
